title: Texas Chili
subtitle: slow-cooked beef chili, no beans
excerpt: Texan chili is all about the beef and the chilli paste -- no beans, no tomato chunks. The meat is cut into cubes, not minced, and cooked low and slow until it falls apart. Serve with soured cream and cornbread.
sourceNotes: Texas chili, or chili con carne, is fiercely debated in the Lone Star State. Purists allow no beans and no tomatoes. The dish traces back to San Antonio chili stands of the late 19th century.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 3 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch and freeze half.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Tastes better the next day once the flavours have melded.

content.text: Brown the beef in batches and do not rush it. Good colour on the meat means deep flavour in the finished chili. Use chuck steak cut into 3cm cubes -- it breaks down beautifully over a long, slow cook.

items.prepNote: use 2 dried ancho chillies, soaked and blended

content.text: Pat the beef dry with kitchen paper. Season all over with salt.
Heat oil in a large heavy pot over high heat. Brown the beef in 3 or 4 batches, giving each piece space in the pan. Each batch needs 2 to 3 minutes per side. Set aside.
Reduce heat to medium. Cook the onion in the same pot for 8 minutes until golden.
Add the garlic, spices, and tomato puree. Stir for 2 minutes.
Return the beef to the pot. Pour in the stock and tinned tomatoes if using. Stir well.
Bring to a boil, then reduce to a very low simmer. Cover and cook for 90 minutes, stirring every 20 minutes.
Remove the lid for the last 20 minutes if the chili needs thickening. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Serve with soured cream, fresh chilli, and cornbread.

items.cause: Too much liquid or lid on the whole time
items.fix: Simmer uncovered for 20 to 30 minutes. The starch from the beef will help it thicken naturally.

items.symptom: Beef is still tough after 90 minutes
items.cause: Heat too low or chuck cut too large
items.fix: Continue cooking for another 30 minutes. Chuck needs time to break down. Keep the simmer steady.

items.cause: Spices added too late or not enough salt
items.fix: Add an extra pinch of cumin and cayenne and simmer for 10 more minutes. Season generously with salt at the end.

content.text: Texas chili has been argued over for more than a century. The official state food of Texas contains no beans and no tomatoes, according to chili purists. The dish grew out of the chili stands of San Antonio in the 1870s, where it was sold cheaply to workers and cowboys. Regional cook-offs still debate the definitive recipe with considerable passion.
